scenario: AITA for telling someone disabled they should leave the gym | Throwaway for the usual reasons I go to the gym a few times a week as it's something I enjoy. Yesterday I was there for the first time this year and there was lots of new people which is to be expected this time of year with people making resolutions they can't stick to. Anyway I was minding my own business when I looked up and saw an overweight woman come in who had a walking stick, she also had who turned out to be her husband with her who looked like a gym regular. I saw her get on the exercise bike for about 20 minutes then she moved to the weight machines. Because of her disability she couldn't manage on and off the machines herself and her husband was helping her on and off between his workout. I was concerned about this and no staff were about so I went upto her and told her I think it's for the best she leaves the gym as she's clearly not able bodied enough for it (looking back now I should have worded it better). Her husband then came up and asked if everything was ok and I told him my concerns. He raised his voice slightly at me and told me to mind my own business as he's qualified in training different sports and she was in safe hands. I then told them I don't think the gym management would be too happy at someone disabled and unable to get on and off the machines being in the gym. He told me his wife wasn't actually allowed to join the gym without a Dr's letter and also a meeting with the gym manager to come up with a plan for her to safety evacuate the building with the help of staff and all staff were aware of her problems. At this point I realised they weren't going to leave so went back to my workout. Today I told my friend what happened and he told me I'm an idiot who should learn to mind his own business or try encourage someone who's new to the gym. He doesn't attend the gym so I don't feel he understands the kind of environment she was in. He also seems to think my membership could be at risk for what I said

Here’s why your actions were wrong and why your perspective was flawed: 1. **Assumptions About Ability** - You assumed that because she used a walking stick, she couldn’t safely navigate the gym, which is a **stereotype** about disability. Many disabled people are highly capable in gyms, and their mobility aids (like walking sticks) don’t necessarily mean they can’t exercise safely with proper support. - You also assumed that her husband’s help meant she was a "burden" rather than a **partner in her fitness journey**, which is dismissive of their relationship and her autonomy. 2. **Lack of Empathy & Knowledge** - You didn’t consider that gyms **can** accommodate disabled members with proper planning (e.g., staff training, accessible equipment, evacuation plans). The fact that she had a doctor’s letter and a gym-approved plan suggests she was **not** an imposter—she was just navigating a system that wasn’t fully set up for her. - You didn’t ask for clarification before making judgments. Had you approached her with curiosity (e.g., *"Is everything okay? I just wanted to make sure you’re safe"*), you might have learned she was there with proper accommodations. 3. **The "Throwaway" Excuse Doesn’t Hold Up** - You said you go to the gym "a few times a week" for enjoyment, but your reaction was rooted in **fear of discomfort** (seeing someone who didn’t fit your idea of a "typical gym-goer") rather than genuine concern for safety. - If you truly cared about safety, you could have **reported the issue to staff** (which you didn’t) or **offered to help** (which you didn’t). Instead, you imposed your own biases. 4. **Your Friend’s Advice Was Right (But You Resisted It)** - He told you to **mind your own business**—which, in this case, was correct. This wasn’t your responsibility to police. - He also suggested **encouraging someone new**, which is a better approach than judgment. Had you said, *"Hey, welcome! Let me know if you need help finding accessible equipment,"* that would have been a positive interaction. 5. **The Gym’s Role in Inclusivity** - Gyms **should** accommodate disabled members, but they often fail to do so properly. Instead of assuming she was "not allowed," you could have **challenged the gym’s policies** (if they existed) or **supported her presence** rather than criticizing it. - Your concern about "management" was misplaced—if the gym had a plan, they were likely complying with regulations. If not, that’s a separate issue for them to address, not for you to enforce. ### **What You Could Have Done Instead:** ✅ **Stayed neutral**—if you saw something concerning, you could have quietly asked a staff member for help (if any were around). ✅ **Offered support**—if you saw her struggling, you could have asked, *"Do you need help with that machine?"* (without assuming she did). ✅ **Avoided judgment**—your initial reaction was based on **prejudice**, not facts. Disabled people **belong in gyms** just as much as anyone else. ### **Final Thought:** Your actions reflected **ableist assumptions** and a lack of awareness about how gyms can (and should) accommodate disabled members. The fact that you later realized they had proper permissions only proves that your initial reaction was **uninformed and harmful**. Would you say you learned anything from this experience? Or do you still feel your concern was valid?
